deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, equations or derivations. It is a qualitative natural-philosophy draft. It continues the previous page's question of why the four 'organic' elements O, N, H and C are the universal carriers of life. It then moves to a molecular-physical hypothesis about the states of matter.

(1) Link to the previous page. Riemann supposes that the first property listed there really is what makes these four elements especially suited to life processes. That property is being very hard (or impossible) to condense. If so, this property already makes the factual conditions of life listed under 2) and 3) understandable. It becomes even more so if one traces the phenomena of condensing gases into liquids and solids back to causes.

(2) Hypothesis on condensation. This passage is cancelled by a single long diagonal stroke running from 'Bei der Condensation' to 'Capillarerscheinungen'.
- When a gas condenses, a fixed number of gas atoms join into one 'solid particle' (festes Theilchen). Every particle contains the same number of atoms arranged in the same way.
- These particles carry noticeable cohesion and adhesion forces. They can also carry noticeable electrical (electrostatic) forces.
- A liquid consists of such solid particles floating in an elastic fluid. A marginal addition says this fluid is the particles' own gaseous dissolution, i.e. their vapour, possibly mixed with other gases.
- The particles survive only while the surrounding gas exerts a certain pressure on them. Below a minimum pressure p_min they turn into gas.
- For a given substance, p_min is a definite function of temperature and increases with T. In modern terms this is a vapour-pressure (saturation) curve p_min = p_s(T) with dp_s/dT > 0.
- In liquids, the pressure the particles need is always supplied by external forces; cohesion alone does not suffice. Cohesion forces account for capillary phenomena.
- In solids, cohesion forces alone produce a pressure high enough to keep the particles in existence.

(3) Classification of forces on (simple or compound) chemical atoms.
- Forces tending to bring atoms together: (a) external forces, i.e. pressure; (b) cohesion and adhesion forces, jointly called 'capillary forces'.
- Forces tending to push them apart: (a) thermal repulsion; (b) chemical repulsion.

(4) Gaseous state. Thermal repulsion, helped by chemical repulsion, balances the external pressure. Chemical repulsion and capillary forces act only in a subordinate way. Chemical repulsion shows itself when gases mix; capillary forces act at the boundary where solids and liquids are in contact.

The next page continues with the liquid state, where capillary forces alone, without external pressure, cannot balance the repulsive forces. In modern shorthand the scheme is an equilibrium condition p_ext + P_cap = P_therm + P_chem, with different dominant terms in each state of aggregation. This shorthand is mine, not Riemann's.
errors: Physically obsolete: a liquid is not a suspension of 'solid particles' in their own vapour. This is a pre-kinetic, caloric-style picture, with 'thermal repulsion' treated as a force.

The claim that in liquids cohesion alone can never supply the needed pressure, so external pressure is always required, conflicts with later knowledge. Van der Waals internal pressure is large, and liquids can sustain negative pressure (tension).
The qualitative claim that the minimum pressure is fixed for a given substance and temperature and rises with T is correct in substance, as the analogue of the vapour-pressure curve.

results.what: Hypothesis that liquids and solids consist of fixed aggregates of gas atoms. Liquids are such particles in their own vapour, stable only above a temperature-dependent minimum pressure that increases with T.
results.modern_name: Qualitative vapour-pressure / saturation curve; molecular-cluster picture of condensation
results.usually_credited_to: Vapour-pressure law: Dalton, Regnault; thermodynamics: Clapeyron (1834), Clausius (1850)

results.what: Classification of interatomic causes into attractive ones (external pressure, capillary = cohesion + adhesion) and repulsive ones (thermal, chemical), with the state of aggregation set by which forces balance.
results.modern_name: Pre-kinetic force-balance theory of states of matter (cf. later van der Waals internal pressure)
results.usually_credited_to: Laplace/caloric tradition; van der Waals (1873) for the quantitative theory

deep.surprise_reason: This is speculative natural philosophy typical of mid-19th-century chemistry and physics, with no mathematical content. Riemann's Naturphilosophie fragments are known, partly published in the Werke. It is a minor unpublished detail, and part of it is cancelled.

checkable.sympy: diff(p0*exp(-L/(R*T)), T) > 0  (with L, R, T, p0 positive)
checkable.asserts: A Clausius–Clapeyron-type vapour pressure p_s(T) rises with temperature, matching Riemann's qualitative claim that the minimum pressure increases with T.

transcription_corrections: Line 1–2: 'schwer zerlegt werden zu können' should probably read 'schwer verdichtet werden zu können' (hard to condense). This matches the first property named on the previous page.
'diese neuen Elemente' should probably read 'diese vier Elemente' (the four organic elements).
'Lebensprozessen[?] zu dienen' is plausibly 'Lebensprocessen zu dienen'.
The section from 'Bei der Condensation' to 'Capillarerscheinungen' is cancelled by a long diagonal stroke. The transcription does not mark this.
'eine dreifache[?] Ursache' is doubtful; the text goes on to list two classes (approaching and separating causes), so 'zweifache' or another word is possible.
Bottom margin should read approximately: 'erstere bei der Mischung der Gase, letztere an der Grenze von festen Körpern und liquiden Flüssigkeiten'.
